title: Best Personal CRM for Real Estate Agents in 2026
summary: The best personal CRM for real estate agents keeps past clients warm for a decade. Dex, Cloze, Follow Up Boss, and Wise Agent compared with 2026 pricing.
body_markdown:
Search for the best CRM for[real estate agents](https://getdex.com/realestate/) and nearly every result is a lead machine. Portal integrations, round-robin routing, speed-to-lead dialers, twelve-touch drip campaigns for strangers who filled in a form at 11 p.m. That software is real and it works, but it is aimed at the part of the business that is getting smaller.


The bigger part is people you already know. In NAR's 2026 Member Profile, the typical Realtor earned 28% of their 2025 business from repeat clients and another 22% from referrals by past clients ([NAR, 2026 Member Profile](https://www.nar.realtor/news/economists-outlook/the-feature-sheet-2026-member-profile) ). Half the book comes from the sphere.


And the sphere moves slowly. Sellers in NAR's 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers had owned their homes for a median of 11 years before selling, the longest on record ([NAR, 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers](https://www.nar.realtor/news/economists-outlook/top-10-takeaways-from-nars-2025-profile-of-home-buyers-and-sellers) ). The job is not converting a lead in five minutes. It is still being the agent someone thinks of a decade after closing.


That is a personal CRM job. Here is how the main options handle it, including two that are really lead engines, so you can tell which kind you are buying.


## **Fast facts:**


-


[Dex](https://getdex.com/) is the best personal CRM for agents whose business runs on past clients and referrals: $12/month for Premium or $20/month for Professional on annual billing, with a 7-day free trial.


-


[Cloze](https://www.cloze.com/app/pricing) is the closest thing to a personal CRM built for agents. Pro is $17/month, but text message syncing starts at Business Gold ($29/user/month) and drip campaigns at Platinum ($42/user/month).


-


[Follow Up Boss](https://www.followupboss.com/pricing) is a lead-conversion CRM for teams buying online leads, from $58/user/month on annual billing ($69 monthly).


-


[Wise Agent](https://wiseagent.com/pricing.asp) is a budget all-in-one with transaction management at $42/month annual or $49 monthly, covering up to five team members on a shared login.


-


The real question is not which CRM has the most features. It is whether your business comes from strangers or from people you already know.


Let's dive in deeper.


## What a personal CRM does for a real estate agent


A real estate CRM is organized around where a lead sits in the funnel. A personal CRM is organized around a person and how long it has been since you talked. For an agent working a sphere, that second shape does four jobs.


-


**Capture without typing.** It pulls contacts and conversations from email, calendar, LinkedIn, and messaging apps, so the history builds itself instead of depending on what you remembered to log at 9 p.m.


-


**A cadence per person.** Past clients every quarter, top referral partners every month, the wider sphere twice a year. The software tracks who is due.


-


**Dates that matter to them.** Closing anniversaries, birthdays, a kid leaving for college. Each one is a reason to reach out that is not a sales pitch.


-


**Context at the moment you reach out.** When the reminder fires, the note that they wanted a bigger yard is on the same screen.


What is missing from that list is just as telling: lead routing, IDX websites, drip campaigns, transaction checklists. Those matter, but they serve the front of the funnel. The tools below differ mostly in how much of that front-of-funnel machinery they bundle, and what you pay for it.


## The best personal CRMs for real estate agents


### 1. Dex: best for sphere and past-client follow-up


*Dex's landing page. Photo taken from: getdex.com*


Dex is a personal CRM built around the relationship rather than the deal. It pulls contacts from Gmail, Outlook, Google Calendar, LinkedIn, WhatsApp, and more (see:[integrations](https://getdex.com/integrations/) ), merges them into one timeline per person, then puts a keep-in-touch cadence on the people who matter.


*Timeline view in Dex*


Several pieces map directly onto an agent's week.


Keep-in-touch reminders handle the sphere. Put past clients in a group on a 90-day cadence and referral partners on 30, and Dex surfaces who is due each morning. A synced email or message to that person resets the clock, so you are not logging touches by hand.


Dated reminders cover closing anniversaries, the cleanest excuse an agent has to check in without asking for anything. Reminders can repeat every year, so each anniversary comes back on its own.


Map view puts your contacts on a map. When you list a house, you can see which past clients and sphere contacts live nearby before you send the just-listed note. Filter the map by group to narrow it to your farm area or to past clients only.


*Dex's Map View*


*Filtering Dex's Map View by group*


The card scanner handles the open house. Point your phone at a business card and Dex turns it into a contact, so the people you met on Sunday are in your sphere before you lock up.


*Dex's card scanner*


Voice notes capture a showing while it is fresh.[Dictate a note](https://youtube.com/shorts/uMtpYFZlpMo?si=kAPOyDWEHoWxWKnW) from the car and one-click AI Cleanup tidies it into a proper note, before you forget what the buyer said about the kitchen.


*Note creation with AI Cleanup in Dex*


Profile sharing saves the retyping. When someone new turns up on LinkedIn or Instagram,[share their profile straight into Dex](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/dcIxmi4VAPA) instead of copying details across.


Job change alerts come through LinkedIn sync. A past buyer who gets promoted into a role in another city is about to sell one house and buy another, and that alert is often the first you hear of it.


Custom fields and notes hold the rest: closing date, property address, lender, the school district they cared about, the dog's name.


Mail merge, on the Professional plan, can pull those custom fields into an email, so one send drops each client's closing date or address into their house-anniversary note.


Dex Shuffle is for the slow afternoon. Tap the dice icon and it picks someone worth reaching out to, then drafts a few short messages you can edit.


Dex also goes where you already work: a[browser extension](https://getdex.com/browser-extension) for Gmail, Facebook, Instagram, and X,[mobile](https://getdex.com/mobile) and[desktop](https://getdex.com/desktop) apps, and an[MCP connection](https://getdex.com/ai-agents) that lets AI assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT work with your contacts.


Where Dex stops: it has no lead routing, no IDX website, no drip campaigns, no transaction management, and no dialer. Mail merge is on Professional, not Premium. If you buy portal leads, Dex is not the tool that catches them.


**Pricing:** $12/month for Premium and $20/month for Professional on annual billing, with a 7-day free trial.


### 2. Cloze: best if you want relationships and marketing in one app


*Cloze's landing page. Photo taken from: cloze.com*


Cloze began as a relationship manager that captured email, calls, and meetings automatically, and over the last few years it has turned hard toward agents and brokerages (our[Cloze CRM review](https://getdex.com/blog/cloze-crm-review/) covers the history). The core is still good: it builds contact history without data entry, and it reminds you when it is time to reach out to key people.


The catch is where the agent features sit. Cloze Pro, the individual plan, is $17/month billed annually or $19.99 month to month. Syncing text messages from iOS and Android starts at Business Gold, $29 per user per month. Drip campaigns, lead capture, the listing-matching engine with MLS and IDX support, marketing email, and automatic newsletters are on Business Platinum at $42 per user per month. Most agent conversations happen over text, so the realistic starting price for an agent is Gold.


There is a 14-day free trial with no card, after which accounts drop to a limited free plan.


**Best for:** a solo agent or small team that wants sphere nurture and marketing in one place and is comfortable paying roughly $350 to $500 per person a year for it.


### 3. Follow Up Boss: best if your business really runs on online leads


*Follow Up Boss's landing page. Photo taken from: followupboss.com*


Follow Up Boss is not a personal CRM, and it does not pretend to be. It is here because it is the default answer agents hear, and because for some agents it is the right one.


It is built for speed to lead. It connects to more than 200 lead sources, distributes leads by round robin or first to claim, runs automated action plans, and lets agents call, text, and email from inside the app. Grow is $58 per user per month billed annually or $69 monthly, with calling as a $33 to $39 add-on. Pro is $416 a month billed annually and includes 10 users. Every plan starts with a 14-day free trial.


If you pay for Zillow or other portal leads every month, this is the category you are shopping in. For a sphere-driven agent, smart lists and action plans can approximate keep-in-touch cadences, but you are paying for machinery built to work strangers.


### 4. Wise Agent: best budget all-in-one with transaction management


*Wise Agent's landing page. Photo taken from: wiseagent.com*


Wise Agent is a traditional real estate CRM at a low flat price: $49/month, or $42/month on annual billing ($499 a year), with up to five team members on a shared login. That includes drip campaigns, lead automation, a landing page, transaction management, and 100 lead enhancement credits. Texting is an add-on called WiseText at $11/month plus an $80 one-time registration fee. There is a 14-day trial.


It suits an agent who wants one inexpensive system to run contacts and the transaction checklist together. The trade-off is that relationship follow-up is one module in a wide product, so it takes more setup to get the per-person cadence a personal CRM starts with.


### 5. Your phone's contacts and calendar


Free, already installed, and genuinely fine for a newer agent with a small sphere. It stops working once you can no longer remember who you last spoke to or what about, which for most agents is somewhere in the low hundreds of contacts. There is no history, no cadence, and nothing to tell you who has gone quiet.

## What a year of past-client follow-up looks like


Take an agent eight years in, with 180 past clients and 40 referral partners: lenders, inspectors, attorneys, a couple of contractors.


In a personal CRM, past clients go on a 90-day cadence, the top 20 referral partners on 30 days, and the other 20 on six months. That works out to about 1,000 touches a year, roughly 19 a week, or four a workday. Most take under two minutes, because the last real conversation is on the screen.


Layer on 180 closing anniversaries spread across the year and a handful of job change alerts. None of it is a campaign. It is short notes that reference something real, which is exactly what a drip sequence cannot do.


*Dex's Keep-In-Touch Kanban Board*


Over eleven years, a quarterly cadence adds up to about 44 conversations with each past client before the median one sells. The agent who had those conversations is the one who gets the call.


## How to choose


-


If most of your business comes from past clients and referrals, start with a personal CRM. Dex is the lowest-cost way to put every past client on a cadence.


-


If you buy leads every month, buy a lead CRM. Follow Up Boss is the standard for teams. Some agents run it for leads and a personal CRM for clients after closing, which works as long as you decide which tool owns a contact once the deal closes.


-


If you want one app and will pay for it, Cloze Business Gold or Platinum bundles relationship tracking with texting and marketing.


-


If budget is tight and you want the transaction checklist in the same place, Wise Agent covers a lot for $42 to $49 a month.


-


Check what your brokerage already provides before paying for a second lead tool. Brokerage CRMs tend to be strong on leads and thin on the personal sphere, and that gap is the one worth filling.


## Who this isn't for


-


If your brokerage requires every contact to live in the company CRM, a personal CRM alongside it just creates a second copy to go stale.


-


If you run a team that needs lead routing, ISA handoffs, and accountability reporting, you want a lead CRM first. We explain the split in[personal CRM vs sales CRM](https://getdex.com/blog/dex-vs-pipedrive/) .


-


If you are an investor tracking brokers, lenders, and sellers rather than clients, read our[CRM for real estate investors comparison](https://getdex.com/blog/dex-vs-affinity-crm-real-estate-investors/) instead.


-


If you manage tenants, leases, and maintenance, that is property management software. A personal CRM will not do it and should not try.


## Choosing a personal CRM as a real estate agent


Half of a typical agent's business now comes from people they have already served or the people those clients send. Those relationships pay out slowly, often a decade after the first closing, and nothing about a lead-conversion CRM is designed to keep them warm that long.


A personal CRM is. If your sphere is where your business comes from, start there, and add lead tooling only if you are actually buying leads.[Start your free 7-day Dex trial.](https://getdex.com/pricing/?ref=blog&ref_post=best-personal-crm-for-real-estate-agents)

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is the best personal CRM for real estate agents?


For agents whose business comes mostly from past clients and referrals, Dex is the best fit at $12 a month on annual billing. It captures conversations from email, calendar, LinkedIn, and messaging, and puts each past client on a keep-in-touch cadence. Cloze is the stronger pick if you want marketing and texting bundled in and will pay $29 to $42 per user per month for it.


### What is the difference between a personal CRM and a real estate CRM?


A real estate CRM is organized around leads and transactions: lead sources, routing, drip campaigns, and deal stages. A personal CRM is organized around people and time since last contact: cadences, dated reminders, and a timeline of every conversation. Most agents need the first for the front of the funnel and the second for the sphere.


### How often should real estate agents contact past clients?


Common practice is a personal touch every quarter, plus the closing anniversary and birthday. With sellers now staying in a home a median of 11 years, consistency over a long stretch matters more than intensity in the months after closing.


### Is Cloze or Dex better for real estate agents?


Cloze bundles marketing, drip campaigns, and MLS listing matching, but text syncing starts at $29 per user per month and campaigns at $42. Dex skips marketing automation and costs $12 a month for automatic capture and keep-in-touch cadences. Choose Cloze for one app that does everything, Dex for the sphere handled cheaply and well. Our[Dex vs Cloze comparison](https://getdex.com/blog/dex-vs-cloze/) goes deeper.


### Can I use a personal CRM alongside Follow Up Boss or my brokerage CRM?


Yes. Many agents let the lead tool handle new inquiries and the personal CRM hold the relationship after closing. Decide up front which system owns a contact at each stage so you do not end up with two copies going stale.


### How much should a real estate agent spend on a CRM?


Personal CRMs like Dex run $12 to $20 a month. Cloze runs $17 to $42 per user per month depending on tier. Wise Agent is $42 to $49 a month flat. Follow Up Boss starts at $58 to $69 per user per month before calling. Spend on lead tooling in proportion to what you spend on leads.
